items.stem: Hydrogen-1 and hydrogen-3 are isotopes. Explain what this means and why they have the same chemical properties.
items.answer: Same number of protons (1) but different numbers of neutrons (0 and 2). Chemical properties depend on electrons, and both have 1 electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same protons; 1 mark: different neutrons; 1 mark: same electron arrangement → same chemistry.

items.stem: Uranium-235 and uranium-238 are isotopes. Explain what this means and why they have the same chemical properties.
items.answer: Same number of protons (92) but different numbers of neutrons (143 and 146). Chemical properties depend on electrons, and both have 92 electrons.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same protons; 1 mark: different neutrons; 1 mark: same electron arrangement → same chemistry.

items.stem: The nuclide oxygen-16 is written as O with nucleon number 16 and proton number 8. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom.
items.answer: 8 protons, 8 neutrons, 8 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 8; neutrons = A − Z = 8; electrons = protons in neutral atom = 8.

items.stem: The nuclide iodine-131 is written as I with nucleon number 131 and proton number 53. State the number of protons, neutrons and electrons in a neutral atom.
items.answer: 53 protons, 78 neutrons, 53 electrons
items.markingKey: protons = Z = 53; neutrons = A − Z = 78; electrons = protons in neutral atom = 53.

items.stem: Describe the alpha-particle scattering experiment and explain how its results led scientists to replace the "plum pudding" model of the atom with the nuclear model.
items.answer: Alpha particles were fired at thin gold foil in a vacuum; detectors recorded deflections. Most passed straight through (mostly empty space), some were deflected (positive charge concentrated), a very few bounced back (tiny dense nucleus with most of the mass). The plum-pudding model, with spread-out positive charge, predicted only tiny deflections, so it was replaced.
items.markingKey: 1 mark set-up; 3 marks for the three observations with conclusions; 1 mark why plum pudding fails.

items.stem: A very small number of alpha particles bounced back. What did this show?
options: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
items.answer: The atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus
items.markingKey: Large deflections need a concentrated positive charge and mass.

items.stem: Nuclear fission is
options: the loss of electrons from an atom
the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei
the joining of two small nuclei
the emission of an alpha particle
items.answer: the splitting of a large nucleus into two smaller nuclei
items.markingKey: Fission: U-235 absorbs a neutron and splits, releasing energy and 2–3 neutrons.

items.stem: Explain how a chain reaction occurs in uranium-235.
items.answer: A neutron is absorbed by a U-235 nucleus, which splits releasing energy and 2 or 3 neutrons; these can be absorbed by further U-235 nuclei, causing more fissions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: neutron absorbed and fission; 1 mark: neutrons released cause further fissions.

items.stem: State one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion.
items.answer: Both release large amounts of energy from the nucleus (mass converted). Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each.

items.stem: In a reactor, each fission releases on average 2.4 neutrons. Explain what fraction of these must, on average, go on to cause another fission for steady power, and how control rods affects the reactor.
items.answer: Exactly one neutron per fission must cause another (the rest are absorbed or escape). Control rods absorb neutrons to set this rate; the moderator slows neutrons so they cause fission; the coolant removes heat to the boiler.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one per fission; 1 mark: role of named component.

items.stem: Stars such as the Sun release energy in their cores. (a) Explain how a chain reaction is controlled. (b) Explain why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth.
items.answer: (a) Control rods absorb some of the neutrons so that on average one neutron from each fission causes another. (b) Very high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei; hard to contain.

items.stem: Stars such as the Sun release energy in their cores. (a) Explain why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth. (b) State one advantage and one disadvantage of fission power compared with burning fossil fuels.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the moderator is needed in a thermal fission reactor. (b) State one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion.
items.answer: (a) It slows down the fast neutrons released, because slow (thermal) neutrons are much more likely to be absorbed by U-235 and cause fission. (b) Both release large amounts of energy from the nucleus (mass converted). Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) State one similarity and one difference between fission and fusion. (b) Explain where the energy released in fission comes from.
items.answer: (a) Both release large amounts of energy from the nucleus (mass converted). Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei. (b) The total mass of the products is slightly less than the original nucleus plus neutron; the lost mass is released as energy.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. (b) [2]

items.stem: In a reactor, each fission releases on average 2.4 neutrons. Explain what fraction of these must, on average, go on to cause another fission for steady power, and how the coolant affects the reactor.
items.answer: Exactly one neutron per fission must cause another (the rest are absorbed or escape). Control rods absorb neutrons to set this rate; the moderator slows neutrons so they cause fission; the coolant removes heat to the boiler.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one per fission; 1 mark: role of named component.

items.stem: A nuclear power station uses uranium-235 as fuel. (a) Describe nuclear fusion and state where it occurs naturally. (b) Explain why fusion is difficult to achieve on Earth.
items.answer: (a) Two light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus (helium), releasing energy; in stars. (b) Very high temperature and pressure are needed to overcome repulsion between positive nuclei; hard to contain.
